project.author: WhyOS-Apps contributors
project.description: BARbarious shows your texts as barcodes and QR codes for a scanner to read.

project.name: BARbarious

whyos.changelog: The status bar comes from WhyOS now, so the app no longer draws its own.
whyos.description:
Keep the codes you show often, such as a Wi-Fi login, a ticket, a
product number or a login for a barcode scanner, and show them on the
badge's screen for a scanner or a phone to read. Control characters
such as Tab and Enter can be part of a code.

Showing a code:
- Choose it in the list and press Enter. The code is as big as the
  screen allows; the screen goes to full brightness and stays on while
  the code shows, up to 10 minutes after the last key.
- Left and Right go to the previous and next code.

Quick code, the list's first row: type a text and see its code at once.
It is not saved; Enter keeps it as a code of the list.

Making a code: the triangle adds one, the cross edits it, and the
square has the other options (show, edit, type, move, delete). A code
has a name for the list, a type and a text of up to 1000 characters.
In the text:
- Tab puts in a TAB, Shift+Enter a CR (LF or CR LF in the settings).
- Ctrl with a letter puts in ^A to ^Z; Ctrl+] is GS.
- The square puts in any other control character, or GS1's FNC1: type
  its name to find it.
- The triangle chooses the type. Next to each type it says what the
  text needs of it: some take digits only, and Code 39 needs a scanner
  with Full ASCII on for lower case and control characters.

Types: QR Code, Data Matrix, Aztec, PDF417, Code 128, Code 39, EAN-13,
UPC-A, ITF and Codabar.

Settings (cloud key): the type of a new code, QR's error correction,
the quiet zone, what Shift+Enter puts in, the text under a barcode and
full brightness.

The codes are stored as plain text on the badge, so do not save
passwords in them.

launch.info: texts as barcodes and QR codes

whyos.summary: BARbarious shows your texts as barcodes and QR codes for a scanner to read.

whyos.changelog: Built on the WhyOS SDK: the drawn keypad is gone, the line and its result sit under the roll of earlier sums, the angle unit is kept, and the circle, clover and diamond work as in every app.
whyos.description:
Type a sum on the keyboard; its result shows as you type, and Enter (or =)
works it out and puts it on the roll above. Up and Down bring earlier sums
back to change them. Starting with + * / ^ % or ! goes on from the last
answer, and an x after a number means times.

It knows + - * / ^, brackets, n% (n/100), n! and mod; pi, e and ans
(the last answer); sqrt, cbrt, abs, exp, ln, log, log2, sin, cos, tan,
asin, acos, atan, sinh, cosh, tanh, round, floor and ceil. 2pi and
3(4+5) multiply. Numbers can be written as 0xff, 0b1010 or 1.5e3, and a
whole-number answer also shows in hexadecimal and binary.

Angles are in degrees; Tab switches to radians, as the setting (the clover
key) does, and the choice is kept. The circle key shows the sums worked
out, the diamond the keys. Esc clears the line, and on an empty line
closes the calculator, as the logo key does.
whyos.summary: Type a sum, get the answer: functions, hex and binary

project.author: WhyOS-Apps contributors
project.description: HIDeous lets you control your computer using pre-recorded input from your badge.
project.license_type: MIT AND OFL-1.1 AND LGPL-2.1-or-later
project.name: HIDeous

whyos.changelog: The status bar comes from WhyOS now, so the app no longer draws its own.
whyos.description:
The badge as a USB keyboard and mouse for a computer. Save texts you
type often, such as an address, a long command or a login sequence,
and let the badge type them.

Typing a text:
- Connect the computer to the badge's bottom USB-C port, and unplug the
  side port: while it is connected, the computer does not see the badge.
- Click where the text should go, choose the text in the list and press
  Enter. Esc stops the typing.

Making a text: the triangle adds one, the cross edits it, and the
square has the other options (type, edit, move, delete). A text has a
name for the list and up to 1000 bytes. In the editor:
- Shift+Enter starts a new line, Tab types a tab.
- Shift with Esc, Backspace or an arrow puts in that key.
- Ctrl or Alt with a key puts in that shortcut, such as Ctrl+C.
- The square puts in any other key or shortcut, such as F5, Win+R or
  Ctrl+Alt+Delete.
- The triangle puts in a pause of half a second, for example to let a
  window open after Win+R. Press it again for a longer pause.

Keyboard layout: the badge sends keys, not letters, so set the
computer's layout in the settings (cloud key): US, US International or
US on a Mac. With other layouts, such as German or French, some
characters come out wrong. Accented letters and the euro sign work with
the last two, but you can only add them by editing snippets.txt over
SSH.

Mouse: open the first row of the list. The arrows move the pointer
(tap for one pixel, hold to go faster), Enter is the left button (hold
it to drag), the cross is a right click and Fn+Up/Down scrolls. Keep
awake (the triangle) nudges the pointer every 30 seconds while the app
is open, so the computer does not lock or show you as away. The mouse
needs WhyOS from 2026-10-20 or later.

The texts are stored as plain text on the badge, so do not save
passwords in them.

launch.info: type saved texts, move the mouse

whyos.summary: HIDeous lets you control your computer using pre-recorded input from your badge.

project.author: Damien P. George and the MicroPython contributors, badge port
project.description: Python 3 on the badge - an interactive prompt and your own scripts
project.license_type: MIT AND (Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-or-later) AND BSD-3-Clause AND Zlib AND LGPL-2.1-or-later
project.name: MicroPython

Badge port (start script, patches, setting, ics, xml)

whyos.changelog: Scripts may do what they can in a shell: MicroPython asks for the system permission, which the sandbox gives it.
whyos.description:
MicroPython is a lean implementation of Python 3. From the menu it opens
the interactive prompt (the REPL): type Python and see the result at
once, with history (arrow keys), Tab completion and automatic
indentation. Ctrl+D closes it, Ctrl+E pastes a block of code. In a shell
(serial console or SSH) "micropython" or "python" starts the prompt in
your own terminal, and "python script.py" runs a script.

Put your scripts in badge/appdata/micropython on the SD card: the prompt
starts there, so "import myscript" runs myscript.py. Files also runs a
.py file under Open with, and leaves the prompt open afterwards. Modules
in the lib folder there can be imported from anywhere, and
"python -m mip install <package>" installs packages from micropython-lib
into it (Wi-Fi needed).

Included: json, re, socket and ssl (HTTPS), requests, asyncio,
hashlib, time, os, math, struct, binascii, deflate, select and more, and
the @micropython.native and viper decorators for fast code. For the
badge: meshcore (MeshCore messages and bots over LoRa, with an example
bot), setting (the badge's settings), ics (calendars from an .ics link,
repeats worked out) and xml.etree.ElementTree (XML as in CPython). Not
included: threads, ffi, and CPython's larger standard library. The heap
is 2 MB; MICROPY_HEAP=4M before the command gives a script more.
whyos.summary: Python 3 on the badge: an interactive prompt and your own scripts

project.author: WhyOS-Apps contributors
project.description: Pins logic analyzer I2C UART and LEDs on the badge or with a Bus Pirate 6.
project.license_type: MIT AND OFL-1.1 AND LGPL-2.1-or-later
project.name: OHMinous

whyos.changelog: The status bar comes from WhyOS now, so the app no longer draws its own.
whyos.description:
Work on circuits from the badge's keypad, with the pins on the badge's
J3 and J7 headers, and with a Bus Pirate 6 on the bottom USB port when
you have one. Each tool has both sources; Tab switches between them.

- Pins: IO0 to IO4 and STROBE as inputs (with a pull-up or pull-down)
  or outputs, a map of both headers, and your own names for the pins.
  With a Bus Pirate: its IO0 to IO7.
- Logic: capture the pins, scroll and zoom, save to /root/capture.bin.
  The badge samples in software, up to 50 kHz; a Bus Pirate captures 8
  channels up to 50 MHz.
- Buses: scan the I2C bus on J7, read and write a device's registers,
  or talk to a serial device on IO3 (TX) and IO4 (RX) at 1200 to 19200
  baud. SPI and 1-Wire need a Bus Pirate.
- LEDs: the WS2812 LEDs on J7, or a Bus Pirate's WS2812 and APA102
  strips.
- Power: the headers' supply pins; a Bus Pirate's supply (0.8 to 5.0 V,
  with a current limit) and pull-ups.
- Serial: a terminal to a USB serial adapter on the bottom port, or to
  the Bus Pirate's own.

The circle key shows a log of what the tools sent and read, the cloud
the settings, the diamond the help. Esc goes back, and closes OHMinous
from the start screen; pins it made outputs go back to inputs.

The badge's pins are 3.3 V: do not connect 5 V signals to them.
whyos.summary: Pins, logic analyzer, I2C, UART and LEDs on the badge, or with a Bus Pirate 6.

project.author: RRG/Iceman Proxmark3 contributors, badge build
project.description: Proxmark3 client - read write and sniff RFID and NFC cards from the badge

whyos.description:
The Proxmark3 client (RRG/Iceman) on the badge itself, for a Proxmark3
on the bottom USB port: work with LF and HF cards from the badge's
keyboard, without a laptop. Tested with a Proxmark3 RDV4.

From the menu it opens on its own screens: search for a card, check the
keys of a MIFARE Classic sector by sector and dump it, keep the cards you
saved with a name, their dumps and keys (also the dumps the client saves
itself, iCLASS, Ultralight, ISO 15693, T55xx and more), edit a saved dump in
Write or duplicate it to keep the original, choose the key
lists to try (and edit your own in Write), sniff a reader and a card, and
the client's command line on the screen (Console).

The Proxmark3 needs RRG/Iceman firmware of the same release as this
client (v4.21611); flash it from a computer.

badge's memory. Left out: Lua and Python scripts, and MIFARE Classic key
recovery that runs in the client (nested, darkside, hardnested). Key
checks that run on the Proxmark3 itself (hf mf chk, hf mf fchk) work,
with the default key lists included. The arrow keys recall earlier
commands and move the cursor; Tab does not complete.

The app connects to the Proxmark3 by itself, also when it is plugged in
later. Dumps, key files and traces go to /root/.proxmark3/dumps, in the
badge's flash; your key lists to /root/.proxmark3/dictionaries. In a
shell over SSH or the serial console, pm3 (or proxmark3) starts the
client's command line.

controls it. The session is not encrypted: use it on your own network or
the cable. There is no pointer, only the keys.

whyos.description:
Write notes and documents on the badge, with headings, lists, bold,
italic and underline, saved as markdown (.md) that any other editor can
open. Markdown works while you type: "# " makes a heading, "- " a list,
**bold** turns bold when you type the last star. The cross key shows the
markdown itself.

Code and other text open in a code view with line numbers, colours for
Python, shell, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, YAML, C and more, and Tab
and Enter keep the indent. The triangle runs a Python or shell script
in a terminal window, or shows an HTML page in NetSurf.

Select with Fn and the arrows, copy, cut and paste between documents,
find and replace, full screen for long texts. Files opens .md and .txt
files in Write. The logo key saves before going back to the menu.
whyos.summary: Write notes and documents, edit text and code
